newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Economists hope Serb telecom deal to boost economy.
newsitem.headline: Economists hope Serb telecom deal to boost economy.

text.p: Serbia on Monday forged a major partnership deal by selling a part of its telecom to Italian and Greek firms for almost $1 billion and economists said the funds will breathe life into the ailing economy if spent as promised.

Analysts said Serbia was forced to sell the most lucrative part of its economy in an election year for which it set too optimistic growth targets and hoping to ensure economic progress by rejoining the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

"The government has probably done the best it could under the circumstances. The sale was forced by the fact that there will be no IMF money this year," chief economist of the IZIT Market Research Institute Slobodan Milosavljevic told Reuters.
"Almost $1 billion equals our M1 money supply. With 80 percent of funds being transferred right away this economy stands a chance," he added.

Serbia's post and telecommunications company PTT Srbije sold earlier today a 49 percent stake in its telecom department to Stet of Italy and OTE of Greece for a total of 1.568 billion German marks ($909.7 million).
Stet bought 29 percent stake for 893 million German marks and OTE paid 675 million German marks to acquire 20 percent stake in the Telekom Srbija.
According to the agreement, 80 percent of the total amount will be paid to the account of the Serbian State Development Fund, while the remainder will be paid in January 1998.
Serbian privatisation minister Milan Beko insisted funds raised through the sale of 49 percent stake in its vital national utility would be paid to Serbian development fund.
"Money raised from a sale of public companies... will be exclusively used to support development and export-oriented programmes," he said.

Economists insisted funds were sufficient to boost the industry's activity, eliminate bottlenecks, stimulate investment activity, public works and finance agriculture which helped the country survive almost four years of isolation under U.N. war-related sanctions.
"There are vast possibilities, but also fears that the money may end up some place else," Milosavljevic said.
He suggested that the government, the Privatisation Ministry and the Serbian Development Fund go public with a detailed spending programme to build confidence.
"They must go public with such a programme because the economy is in a recession and social discontent is growing," Milosavljevic said.
Economists said the government may be tempted to use some of the money to pay overdue pensions and wages to buy social peace ahead of elections.
Analysts cautioned that financing pre-election campaign with Telekom's money would be disastrous, helping politicians score an odd political point, but not solving any problems.
Danilo Sukovic, head of the economic research centre at the Institute of Social Sciences, said the sale was good because new foreign partners will dictate some new rules of the game.
"The government should hurry to sell some of its companies in other sectors too. We must not give in to allegations that the national wealth is being sold cheap," Sukovic said.

Opposition political parties blamed the government for selling its telecoms sector at a price roughly running at $1,200 per phone line and compared it to over $2,600 per line what Hungarian and Czech telecoms fetched in similar deals.
But a Western diplomat said: "They must be happy to get anything for the poor telecom sector. Besides, it is not so cheap to sell for 1.6 billion German marks."
The Institute of Economic Sciences (IEN) cautioned that any allocation of funds must not be conducted through the indebted banking sector before it restructures and consolidates.

"If the money goes to banks before they restructure, there is a danger that most of the capital will be lost. Banks must be separated from big state loss-making companies," IEN said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254 ($ = 1.723 German Marks)
